vignette:
Patient: Mr. L., age 47
Occupation: Park Ranger
Trauma: Son’s life-threatening illness (leukemia, diagnosed 18 months ago)

Mr. L. comes to session straight from his shift, still wearing his khaki uniform shirt with the state park patch on the sleeve. He sits heavily in the chair, the leather creaking under him. He apologizes for being five minutes late, explaining that a family of hikers had stopped him near the trailhead, asking about bear activity. He told them the truth—that there hadn’t been any sightings in weeks—but his heart was hammering the whole time. He doesn’t know why.

The story he tells begins two years ago, in early spring. His son, Kavi, was nine. He remembers the day clearly because he was supposed to be mapping a new trail loop, but Kavi had a fever that wouldn’t break. Mr. L. had taken him to the pediatrician, expecting strep throat. Instead, the doctor used the word “pancytopenia.” Within a week, the word “leukemia” entered their lives. Mr. L. describes the moment the oncologist laid out the treatment plan—18 months of chemotherapy, a bone marrow biopsy, the possibility of relapse—as a kind of implosion. He says he felt the world go silent, like the moment before a rockslide. He stopped hearing the doctor’s voice. He only saw Kavi’s small hand on the hospital bed rail.

For the next fourteen months, Mr. L. took a leave of absence from the park service. He lived in the hospital room. He learned to administer IV flushes, to read the numbers on the blood count chart, to recognize the specific shade of pale that meant a transfusion was needed. He stopped sleeping. He stopped eating meals—just coffee and crackers from the vending machine. He remembers the exact sound of the infusion pump’s alarm. It was a high, repeating chirp. He can still hear it in his head, sometimes, when he is trying to fall asleep.

Kavi is in remission now. He is back in school. He plays soccer again. The doctors say his prognosis is excellent. Mr. L. returned to work six months ago. He thought he would feel relief. Instead, he feels like he is waiting for the other shoe to drop.

In session, Mr. L. describes his days in the park now as a kind of hypervigilant patrol. He is responsible for visitor safety, trail maintenance, and wildlife monitoring. But he finds himself scanning the treeline for threats that aren’t there. He checks the same trail camera three times in a shift. He flinches at the crack of a fallen branch. Last week, a child’s laughter echoed from the picnic area, and he froze. His chest tightened. He had to sit down on a bench and put his head between his knees. He thought it was a flashback—the sound of Kavi laughing in the hospital playroom, right before a lumbar puncture. He cannot separate the safe sounds from the dangerous ones.

His wife, Maya, has told him that he is “different.” He is irritable. He snaps at her for small things—for leaving a light on, for moving his coffee cup. He has stopped going to Kavi’s soccer games. He cannot bear to sit in the stands, watching his son run, because his mind immediately runs a catastrophic film: a slide tackle, a broken leg, a fever, a relapse. The only place he feels a semblance of control is in the park, where he can walk the perimeter, check the locks, ensure the boundaries are secure. But even there, the loop is never finished. He checks the same thing twice, three times, and then goes back to check it again.

He has not told anyone at work about his son. He is the stoic ranger, the one who can handle a bear sighting or a lost hiker. But inside, he feels like a man standing on a high ledge, unable to step back. His score on the PCL-5 is 72, indicating very severe PTSD symptoms. He is not here for a diagnosis, he says. He is here because he is tired of checking the trail cameras. He is tired of hearing the pump alarm in the quiet of his own home. He just wants to feel like the ground is solid again.
